extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students studying real analysis / metric spaces
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts definitions, theorems, and standard properties about metric spaces (continuity, separation axioms, bases, separability, compactness, completeness, connectedness, Baire category) as presented in a textbook chapter. Useful as a checklist of properties one must know or verify about metric spaces and continuous maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of algebraic and coordinate operations (Corollary 2.29)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are continuous functions from X into R^n or C^n then f+g, f−g, scalar multiples c f, componentwise products fg, and coordinate projection maps are continuous; 1/f is continuous on the set where f is nonzero; if functions take values in C then complex conjugation is continuous; max and min are continuous when n = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements are given for real- and complex-valued functions and for vector-valued functions in R^n or C^n. Proofs proceed by expressing these maps as compositions of known continuous maps (use Proposition 2.28a and Corollary 2.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: C(S) as vector and metric subspace of B(S)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a metric space (S,d), C(S) (bounded continuous scalar-valued functions on S) is a vector space and is a vector subspace and a metric subspace of B(S) (bounded scalar-valued functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish usage of 'subspace': this text reserves 'vector subspace' when meaning a subspace in the vector-space sense, and 'metric subspace' when meaning a subspace with the induced metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: T1 property: one-point sets are closed (Proposition 2.30a)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any metric space (X,d), every one-point subset {x} is closed; equivalently, X is a T1 space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: {x} is the intersection of closed balls B(r,x) for r>0 (use earlier corollaries about closed balls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hausdorff property: distinct points separated by disjoint opens (Proposition 2.30b)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any two distinct points x and y in a metric space X there exist disjoint open sets U and V with x∈U and y∈V; i.e., metric spaces are Hausdorff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from properties of open balls and the metric; used repeatedly (e.g., in proofs that compact sets are closed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity: point and disjoint closed set separable by neighborhoods (Proposition 2.30c)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any point x and any closed set F with x∉F, there exist disjoint open sets U and V with x∈U and F⊆V; hence metric spaces are regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of the metric structure and previous separation properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normality: disjoint closed sets separable by neighborhoods (Proposition 2.30d)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any two disjoint closed subsets E and F of a metric space X there exist disjoint open sets U and V with E⊆U and F⊆V; i.e., metric spaces are normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often proved using Urysohn-type constructions or by applying (e) to produce separating continuous functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urysohn-type function: continuous separator for disjoint closed sets (Proposition 2.30e)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any two disjoint closed subsets E and F of X there is a continuous function f : X → [0,1] such that f = 0 exactly on E and f = 1 exactly on F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive proof uses metrics (distance to sets); this yields useful partitions of unity and is used to show metric spaces are normal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of a base for a metric topology (Proposition 2.31)
rubrics_metrics.description: A family B of subsets of X is a base for (X,d) iff (a) every member of B is open, and (b) for each x∈X and each open neighborhood U of x there exists B∈B with x∈B⊆U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical example: the family of all open balls. Use (b) to show every open set is a union of base elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent conditions for separability (Proposition 2.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a metric space (X,d) the following are equivalent: (a) X has a countable base; (b) every open cover of X has a countable open subcover; (c) X has a countable dense subset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalences are proved by constructing countable bases from dense sets (balls with rational radii and centers in the dense set), and conversely applying bases to produce countable subcovers and dense sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: separable metric space
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space satisfying the equivalent conditions of Proposition 2.32 is called separable (i.e., has a countable dense subset or a countable base).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: many classical spaces (R^n, ℓ^2-related examples, spaces of polynomials with rational coefficients) are separable; some spaces (e.g., certain function spaces or uncountable discrete spaces) are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of compactness (beginning of §7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space is compact if every open cover of the space has a finite subcover. A subset E⊆X is compact if it is compact as a subspace (every cover by open sets of X has a finite subcollection whose union contains E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition as the primary notion of compactness; many equivalent formulations follow in metric spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact implies separable (Proposition 2.33)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every compact metric space is separable (has a countable dense subset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from the countability condition equivalent to separability: from any open cover by balls one can extract a finite subcover repeatedly indexed by rational radii to build a countable dense set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact subsets are closed and bounded; closed subsets of compact are compact (Proposition 2.34)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Every compact subset E of a metric space X is closed and bounded. (b) Any closed subset of a compact set is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use nested balls for boundedness and the Hausdorff property to show limit points lie inside compact sets (closedness). For (b) pass to complements and finite subcovers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-intersection property characterization of compactness (Proposition 2.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space X is compact iff every collection of closed subsets of X with the finite-intersection property has nonempty intersection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, complements of such closed collections yield open covers with no finite subcover if the intersection were empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential compactness equivalence (Theorem 2.36)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space X is compact iff every sequence in X has a convergent subsequence (i.e., sequential compactness is equivalent to compactness in metric spaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof shows compact ⇒ sequential compact using closedness arguments, and conversely constructs a countable dense set and extracts subsequences via repeated finite covers (diagonal argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heine–Borel Theorem for R^n (Corollary 2.37)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Euclidean space R^n, every closed bounded set is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to Bolzano–Weierstrass in R^1 by successive coordinate subsequence extraction; converse (compact ⇒ closed and bounded) is Proposition 2.34a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous image of a compact set is compact (Proposition 2.38)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is compact and f : X → Y is continuous, then f(X) is a compact subset of Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preimages of an open cover of f(X) to obtain a finite subcover of X and hence of f(X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme value property on compact sets (Corollary 2.39)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is compact and f : X → R is continuous, then f attains its maximum and minimum values (supremum and infimum lie in f(X)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of f(X) compact in R: closed and bounded, so sup and inf are limits of sequences in f(X) and lie in f(X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous bijection from compact space is a homeomorphism (Corollary 2.40)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is compact and f : X → Y is continuous, one-to-one and onto, then f is a homeomorphism (its inverse is continuous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: inverse image of closed sets are closed because images of closed sets in compact spaces are compact (hence closed); thereby f^{-1} is continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform continuity on compact domains (Proposition 2.41)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is compact and f : X → Y is continuous (metric spaces), then f is uniformly continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proof: for each x pick a δ_x giving ε/2 control, cover X by finitely many such balls, let δ be the minimum of finitely many δ_x's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (Theorem 2.42)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients (degree ≥ 1) has a complex root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof in the text uses compactness of large circles and minimization of |P(z)|; shows global minimum of |P| must be zero by contradiction with constructed polynomials Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Cauchy sequence and completeness; closed subsets are complete iff whole space complete (Proposition 2.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence is Cauchy if for every ε>0 there exists N such that d(x_m,x_n)<ε for m,n≥N. A metric space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges. A subset E of a complete metric space X is complete iff it is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use limit existence in complete X and Corollary 2.23 about limits lying in closed sets to characterize closedness↔completeness for subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: B(S) with uniform metric is complete (Proposition 2.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any nonempty set S, the vector space B(S) of bounded scalar-valued functions on S, with the uniform metric, is a complete metric space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: pointwise limits of Cauchy sequences of bounded functions exist and converge uniformly because of uniform (sup) control.

rubrics_metrics.name: C(S) complete under uniform metric (Corollary 2.45)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a metric space (S,d), the vector space C(S) of bounded continuous scalar-valued functions on S, with the uniform metric, is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C(S) is a closed subspace of complete B(S), hence complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total boundedness + completeness ⇔ compactness (Theorem 2.46)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space X is compact iff it is totally bounded (for any ε>0 finitely many ε-balls cover X) and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: compact ⇒ totally bounded and complete (sequential compactness). Conversely, from total boundedness build nested subsequences in balls of radii 1, 1/2, 1/3,... and diagonalize to produce a Cauchy subsequence which converges by completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique uniformly continuous extension from dense subset (Proposition 2.47)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let D be a dense subset of X, Y complete, and f : D → Y uniformly continuous. Then f extends uniquely to a continuous map F : X → Y, and F is uniformly continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: define F(x)=lim f(x_n) for any sequence x_n in D approaching x; well-definedness, uniqueness, and uniform continuity follow from completeness of Y and uniform continuity of f (standard ε/3 argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of connectedness and connected subsets of R (Proposition 2.48)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space X is connected if it cannot be written as the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets. In R, the connected subsets are exactly the intervals (open, closed, half-open, rays, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof for R: if a set contains two points but omits a point between them, it splits into two nonempty open parts; conversely intervals cannot be split.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous image of connected set is connected (Proposition 2.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is connected and f : X → Y is continuous, then f(X) is connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if f(X) = U ∪ V disjoint open nonempty in Y, then f^{-1}(U), f^{-1}(V) separate X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate Value Theorem as corollary (Corollary 2.50)
rubrics_metrics.description: For real-valued functions of a real variable, the continuous image of any interval is an interval (classical IVT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from connectedness of intervals and the previous proposition about continuous images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of connected sets with a common point is connected (Proposition 2.51)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {E_α} is a family of connected subsets of X and they all contain a common point x_0, then the union ⋃_α E_α is connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: any separation of the union would restrict to a separation of some E_α containing x_0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of a connected set is connected (Proposition 2.52)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E is connected in X then its closure cl(E) is also connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If cl(E) were separable into disjoint opens U and V, points of E (and limit points) force both intersections nonempty contradicting connectedness of E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nowhere dense sets and Cantor set example
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed set is nowhere dense if its interior is empty; its complement is open dense. The Cantor set is given as a standard example of a closed nowhere dense subset of R (constructed by repeatedly removing middle open intervals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard Cantor set (remove middle third iteratively) is closed and nowhere dense; its Lebesgue measure equals the product ∏ (1 − r_n) in the general construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baire Category Theorem (Theorem 2.53)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a complete metric space then (a) the intersection of countably many open dense sets is dense (in particular nonempty), and (b) X is not the union of countably many closed nowhere dense sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs nested balls inside open dense sets and uses completeness to produce a limit point lying in every dense open set. Remark: the intersection in (a) is actually dense, not merely nonempty.
